references.text: In [ref:Matt 21:2-3|Matthew 21:2-3], Jesus gives the same instruction to the disciples to go to the village and find a donkey tied there, in Matthew's parallel account of the entry into Jerusalem.
[ref:Mark 11:2-3|Mark 11:2-3] is Mark's parallel account where Jesus sends two disciples to fetch a colt that is tied, which no one has yet sat on – nearly identical wording to Luke's version.
In [ref:Joh 12:14-15|John 12:14-15], Jesus finds a young donkey and sits on it, fulfilling the prophecy in Zechariah. John's account complements the Synoptics' description of the preparations.

[ref:Sak 9:9|Zechariah 9:9] prophesies that the king of Zion shall come riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey. Jesus' instruction to fetch the colt no one has sat on fulfills this messianic prophecy.

[ref:4 Mos 19:2|Numbers 19:2] describes the requirement for a red heifer that has never borne a yoke – the principle that an animal not yet used is holy and reserved for God's service, parallel to the colt no one had sat on.

In [ref:1 Sam 6:7|1 Samuel 6:7], cows that have never borne a yoke are used to carry the ark of the covenant. The principle of an unused animal for holy service is reflected in Jesus' choice of a colt no one had ridden.

[ref:1 Mos 49:11|Genesis 49:11] in Jacob's blessing of Judah mentions that he ties his donkey to the vine – a messianic text pointing to the coming king, and connecting to the colt that was tied in Luke's account.
